title: Balaam's donkey (Numbers 22:21–35)
hookLine: a donkey sees the angel her master can't, and speaks

lines: THE DONKEY SWERVES, SQUEEZES, LIES DOWN.
cards: A king named Balak is frightened. A huge people, the Israelites, fresh from the desert, has camped on his border.
So he sends for a well-known seer named Balaam, known for blessings and curses that stick: come and curse this people for me, and I'll pay you well. Balaam saddles his donkey and sets out.
On the road, the donkey suddenly swerves into a field. Balaam beats her back. She squeezes against a wall and crushes his foot.
He beats her again. Then she just lies down under him. And Balaam, furious, beats her a third time.

teach.h: WHAT HAVE I DONE UNTO THEE?
teach.b: Then this, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?"

And here's the funny part: Balaam argues back, as if a talking donkey were normal. You've made a fool of me, he says; if I had a sword I'd kill you. She answers, reasonably: haven't I carried you all your life?
Have I ever done this before? He has to admit, no. "Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand."
The donkey had seen it all along, three times.

teach.h: THE SEER IS THE ONE WHO'S BLIND.
teach.b: The well-known seer, the professional who sees what others can't, is the only one on the road who's blind.
And his donkey saved his life: the angel says if she hadn't turned aside, I would have killed you and let her live. The rest is just as surprising.

teach.h: THE CURSE COMES OUT A BLESSING.
teach.b: Balaam goes on to King Balak, climbs the hills three times to curse Israel, and three times blessing comes out of his mouth instead.
One of those blessings, how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, is still said in Jewish morning prayers.

teach.h: HIS NAME ON A WALL IN JORDAN.
teach.b: And in 1967, archaeologists in Jordan found a plaster inscription from around the eighth century before Christ that names Balaam son of Beor as a seer of the gods.

teach.h: THE LORD OPENED THE MOUTH OF THE ASS.
teach.b: The lesson Christians have long drawn: God can speak through anyone. Even a donkey.

how: Christians often tell Balaam's story to children for its humor and to adults as a reminder that God can speak through unlikely voices; the New Testament mentions Balaam and his donkey in 2 Peter.

o: a sacrifice offered to break a curse on Israel
the animal who saw the angel her master missed
a stubborn animal that refused to carry the king

games.q: who's who on the road — tap the pairs.
p: the king who wanted a curse

s: Balaam was shocked that his donkey could talk
he argues right back with her, as if it were normal.
Balaam ends up blessing Israel instead of cursing it
three times he tries to curse, and blessing comes out.
Balaam's name has been found outside the Bible
a plaster inscription found in Jordan in 1967 names Balaam son of Beor.

games.q: you're Balaam. your donkey has swerved, crushed your foot and lain down in the road, and now she's talking to you. what do you do?
games.why: he argues: you've made a fool of me. only after God opens his eyes does he see the angel the donkey saw all along.

practice: Think of the voices you tend to brush off: a child who's too blunt, a coworker, a critic, your own tired body lying down under you in the road. Has one of them been trying to tell you something, maybe more than once?
Picture yourself getting off the donkey and listening, and if you pray, ask to have your eyes opened like Balaam's.

wordCard.voice: Balaam's donkey. She saw the angel in the road three times, while her well-known master saw nothing, and then she spoke.

orig.note: Hebrew: Balaam. His name also appears in an ancient inscription from Deir Alla, in Jordan.

carryVoice: Your line: even a donkey can see. She saw the angel three times before he did. That's day four hundred five.
